div.p: In this paper, we study the problem of temporal consistency maintenance where a certain degree of temporal inconsistency is tolerable. We propose a suite of Statistical More-Less (SML) approaches to tradeoff of quality of service (QoS) of temporal consistency against the number of supported transactions. We begin with a base-line algorithm, SML-BA, which provides the requested QoS of temporal consistency. We then propose SML with Optimization (SML-OPT) to further improve the QoS by better utilizing the excessive CPU capacity. Finally, we enhance SML-OPT with a Slack Reclaiming scheme (SML-SR). The reclaimed slacks are used to process jobs whose required computation time is larger than the guaranteed computation time. Simulation experiments are conducted to compare the performance of these schemes (SML-BA, SML-OPT and SML-SR) together with the deterministic More-Less and Half-Half schemes. Our results show that the SML schemes are effective in trading off the schedulability of transactions and the QoS guaranteed. Moreover, SML-SR performs best and offers a significant QoS improvement over SML-BA and SML-OPT.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Although a lot of work has been devoted to scheduling real-time transactions to meet their deadlines, relatively much less work has been done on maintaining the freshness of real-time data objects [7] [12][13] [15]. Temporal consistency [12] is proposed to define the correctness of real-time data objects. A real-time data object is temporally consistent if its value truly reflects the current status of its corresponding entity in the environment. Update transactions that capture the latest status of the data entities are periodically generated to refresh the values of real-time data objects. The problem of scheduling of update transactions consists of two issues: (1) the determination of the updating period and deadline; and (2) the scheduling of update transactions that share system resources. Minimizing the update workload for maintaining temporal consistency becomes an important design issue. A simple method for maintaining temporal consistency is half-half (HH) scheme [4] in which the update period for a real-time data object is set to be half of its validity interval. To further reduce the update workload, the More-Less (ML) scheme is proposed [16].

To provide deterministically guaranteed temporal consistency for real-time data objects, worst-case computation time of update transactions needs to be known in advance. However, for soft/firm real-time databases, the computation time can be elastic and the worst-case computation time is usually much larger than average required computation. In this paper, we study the problem of temporal consistency maintenance of real-time data objects [16] with the objective to provide statistical quality of service (QoS) guarantee in temporal consistency. We consider a single CPU based real-time database system that handles firm real-time update transactions to maintain temporal consistency. The goal is to design Statistical More-Less (SML) approaches that control the QoS of data freshness, i.e., the ability to adjust the percentage of temporal consistency as a tradeoff for improving the schedulability of update transactions. We first propose the SML baseline algorithm (SML-BA) for providing a requested QoS guarantee in temporal consistency. An admission test is designed to prevent the overload situation from occurring while guaranteeing the required QoS of temporal consistency. Then, SML with Optimization (SML-OPT) is proposed to optimize the total guaranteed QoS in temporal consistency by utilizing the remaining capacity of the processor. Finally, a slack reclaiming scheme, namely SML with Slack Reclaiming (SML-SR), is incorporated into SML-OPT to further improve the QoS provided while maintaining the schedulability of update transactions.

div.head: Temporal Consistency
div.p: Real-time data objects are temporal data, i.e., their values change continuously with time [6] [12]. The correctness of a real-time data object X i depends on the difference between the real-time status S(E i ) of the real world entity E i and the current sampling value Val(X i ) of X i . Absolute consistency is proposed to determine the temporal consistency of a real-time data object based on its update time by assuming that there is an average rate of change in S(E i ). Definition 1. A real-time data object (X i ) at time t is absolutely consistent if its sampling time(st i ) plus the validity interval (V i ) of the data object is not smaller than time t, i.e., st i + V i t.

A data value for real-time data object X i sampled at any time point t will be valid for V i following that time point up to (t + V i ). To maintain temporal consistency of all data objects in a real-time database, update transactions have to be defined for them. The update transactions periodically refresh values of the corresponding real-time data objects before those values expire.

div.head: Deterministic Approaches
div.p: In this section, two deterministic approaches for maintaining temporal validity, namely the Half-Half and More-Less approaches, are reviewed. They are deterministic approaches since their objectives are to ensure that all real-time data objects are temporally consistent. Both approaches use fixed period update transactions to guarantee the temporal consistency of realtime data objects. From here on,

Associated with X i (1 i m) is the validity interval of length V i . Update transaction T i updates the corresponding data object X i . Because each update transaction updates different data objects, no concurrency control is considered for update transactions. We assume that an update transaction always samples the value of a data object at the beginning of its period, and all the first jobs of update transactions are initiated at the same time. We also assume that a job from an update transaction arrives at system without any arrival latency.

An update transaction T i for maintaining temporal consistency can be formally defined as: T i = (C i , D i , P i ), where C i , D i and P i denote the worst-case computation time, relative deadline, and period of transaction T i , respectively. D i of update transaction T i is defined as: D i = Deadline of T i Sampling time of T i . The deadlines of the update transactions are firm deadlines. The design objectives of the deterministic approaches are to determine P i and D i such that the temporal consistency of data object X i can be guaranteed and at the same time all the update transactions are schedulable with minimum CPU workload. In order to ensure that all jobs from the update transactions can meet the deadlines, the computation time assigned to each transaction follows the worst-case computation time of the transactions. Simple execution semantics for periodic transactions is assumed: an update transaction must be executed once every period. However, there is no guarantee on when a job of an update transaction is actually executed within a period. It is assumed that the executions of the transactions are preemptable.

div.head: Half-Half (HH) Approach
div.p: The simplest method for maintaining temporal consistency of real-time data objects is to use the One-One approach in which the period and relative deadline of an update transaction is set to be the data validity interval of the data object to be updated by the update transaction.

However, the problem is that the maximum distance of the beginning of the job from an update transaction and the end of its next job is 2V i . Therefore, the separation of the execution of two consecutive jobs of a transaction can exceed the validity interval (V i ) and the data objects can become temporally invalid under this scheme [16]. To resolve this problem, the period and relative deadline of an update transaction have to be less than or equal to half of the data validity interval [4] [16]. Under the Half-Half approach, the farthest distance (based on the arrival time of a periodic transaction job and the finishing time of its next job) of two consecutive jobs from an update transaction is 2P i . If 2P i V i and D i = P i . Thus the temporal consistency of data object X i is guaranteed as long as the jobs of update transaction T i do not miss their deadlines.

div.head: More-Less (ML) Approach
div.p: To minimize the update workload, More-Less (ML) scheme is proposed to guarantees temporal consistency with much less CPU workload comparing with the Half-Half approach [16]. In ML, there are three constraints to follow for transaction T i (1 i m) provided that all the 1 st jobs of transactions start at the same time [16]: 1. Validity Constraint: the sum of the period and relative deadline of transaction T i always equals V i , the length of the validity interval of the data object updated, i.e., P i + D i = V i , as shown in Figure 1. 2. Deadline Constraint: the period of an update transaction is assigned to be more than half of the validity interval of the data object to be updated by the transaction, while its corresponding relative deadline is assigned to be less than half of the validity interval of the same data object. div.head: Figure 1: Deadlines & Periods in More-Less
div.p: Given a set of update transactions, ML derives the periods and deadlines of the update transactions based on the temporal validity intervals of the real-time data objects and the worst-case computation time of the transactions such that the total CPU workload for update transactions is minimized and the schedulability of the resulting update transactions is guaranteed. In ML, the scheduling of the update transactions is based on the Shortest Validity First (SVF) to ensure that all the update transactions can meet their deadlines. SVF assigns priorities to transactions in the inverse order of validity length and breaks ties in favor of a transaction with more computation time [16].

div.head: Statistical Approaches
div.p: Deterministic schemes, namely Half-Half and More-Less, use the worst-case computation time of transactions for scheduling. This may be unnecessarily pessimistic in soft/firm real-time database systems where the computation time of most jobs of periodic transactions could be significantly less than the worst-case computation times. It is difficult in many scenarios to find a feasible schedule with worst-case computation times such that all of the transactions can meet their deadlines. For many realtime database systems, it is usually acceptable to have certain percentages of real-time transactions missing their deadlines [2]. Thus, it may not need to have a deterministic guarantee in temporal consistency of real-time data objects especially when the cost for achieving this is high. Note that if deterministic guarantee in temporal consistency cannot be achieved, applications may have to occasionally tolerate obsolete data. When such a situation becomes acceptable, we need a statistical approach to control the quality of services (QoS) in terms of data freshness provided by update transactions. QoS is a parameter for adjusting the level of temporal consistency guaranteed as a tradeoff for the schedulability of the system. Definition 2. A x% statistical guarantee in temporal consistency for a data object X i is provided if at least x% jobs of a periodic transaction that updates X i commit by their deadlines over an arbitrarily long period of time.

If x% jobs of the update transaction for data object X i can be guaranteed to commit before their deadlines, the QoS of the real-time data object provided can be statistically guaranteed. For example, a Q i of 0.9 means that 90% of the time object X i are temporally consistent over an arbitrarily long period of time.

div.head: The Base Algorithm (SML-BA)
div.p: In this sub-section, we propose the base algorithm of the Statistical More-Less (SML-BA) approach. Its main purpose is to provide flexibility for tradeoff between the guaranteed QoS of temporal consistency of data objects and the schedulability of the set of update transactions that can be supported in the system.

Unlike More-Less, the Statistical More-Less (SML) scheduling proposed in this paper are for systems where the computation time of the jobs from an update transaction T i varies but follows certain distribution. Transaction computation time distribution can be known a priori by pre-analysis [1][13]. Similar to [1], the SML schemes are developed based on assumptions that (1) the distribution of the computation time of a transaction can be pre-analyzed offline; and (2) once a job of an update transaction is released, its computation time is known.

The main difference between ML and SML-BA is that SML-BA includes an admission test that determines when a job can be admitted, and when to reject a job to guarantee the promised QoS in temporal consistency. Rejecting a job reduces the degree of QoS but it can prevent the system from being overloaded. If the system is overloaded, the guaranteed QoS may not be maintained. div.head: SML with Slack Reclaiming (SML-SR)
div.p: We now extend SML-OPT to further improve the QoS in temporal consistency by adding a reclaim policy on unused slacks of the jobs. We use the term slack to refer to unused computation time that has been guaranteed to the jobs of an update transaction. The extended scheme is called SML with Slack Reclaiming (SML-SR).

div.head: Principles of SML-SR
div.p: The basic idea of SML-SR is that variation in computation times of jobs from transactions can be smoothed through aggregation. We classify the jobs from a transaction into three categories according to their computation times: short jobs, long jobs and over-long jobs. Short jobs are those with computation time c ij c i . c i is the guaranteed computation time of T i derived from SML-OPT. Since the computation time of a short job could be significantly smaller than c i , the slack of (c i c ij ) allocated to T i could be reclaimed for the execution of other long jobs, whose computation times are larger than the guaranteed computation time. The over-long jobs have very large computation times. They have a high probability of missing their deadlines. In order not to waste computation resource on the over-long jobs, they are rejected in the admission test. To determine if a job is over-long, we introduce the upper bound of computation time, i c ˆ, such that if c ij > i c ˆ, the job is an over-long job. The determination for the value of i c ˆ is discussed in Section 4.3.3. The computation time originally assigned to an over-long job can be reallocated to long jobs from other transactions, whose computation time is larger than the guaranteed computation time, i.e. c ij c i , but less than i c ˆ. It is expected that completion of long jobs improves QoS of temporal consistency.

The issues that need to be addressed in SML-SR are: (1) how to determine what long and over-long jobs are; (2) how to assign reclaimed slacks to long jobs; and (3) how to execute a long job with the reclaimed slacks such that QoS guaranteed to lower priority transactions is not affected. In Section 4.3.2, we explain how the questions (2) and (3) are answered by using a slack provider and slack consumer scheme. We then address the first question in Section 4.3.3.

div.head: Slack-Provider and Slack-Consumer
div.p: As jobs are categorized into short, long and over-long jobs, a Job Admission Controller (JAC) is used to admit short and long jobs, and reject over-long jobs. Upon admission of a short job or rejection of an over-long job, slack is available from the job as it does not consume all of the guaranteed computation time. In case of rejection of an over-long job, its slack is exactly the same as its guaranteed computation time. A short job or over-long job is a slack-provider, and a long job that consumes slack from a slack-provider is named slack-consumer.

div.head: Slack Reuse and Slack Transfer
div.p: Slack reuse and slack transfer are cruxes for smoothing the variability in computation times through aggregation. Slack reuse refers to the scheme that a slackconsumer, which is a long-job, consumes unused slacks from slack-providers. Slack reuse reduces the slack from the slack-provider. It can be used not only for higher priority slack-providers and lower priority slackconsumers, but also for lower priority slack-providers and higher priority slack-consumers. Slack transfer happens when a short job consumes unused slack from a slackprovider, which increases slack of the short job while reducing slack from the slack-provider. Slack transfer lends itself to extend the expiration time of the original slack from the slack-consumer. Otherwise, the original slack from the slack-consumer may be wasted due to system idling. div.head: Admission Control
div.p: Upon the admission of a short job or rejection of an over-long job, the Job Admission Controller (JAC) creates a slack-producer job:

(1) If the admitted job J kj is a short job, the controller creates a slack-producer job J SR-k with computation time c SR-k = c k -c kj , priority level = k + ½, and the deadline is set as that of J kj . (2) If J kj is an over-long job, it is rejected and the controller creates a slack-producer job J SR-k with computation time c SR-k = c k , priority level = k + ½, and the deadline is set as that of J kj . Note that the slack-producer job J SR-k has a lower priority than the original transaction T k . Admitted long jobs are slack-consumers since their executions require additional computation time from the slack-providers. Reducing the priority level by ½ (a lower priority) is to make a slack-provider have the same priority as the original transaction comparing with other transactions, however, it has a lower priority comparing with the original transaction.

The admitted jobs and the created slack-producer jobs are queued at the job queue according to their assigned priorities. When a slack-producer job is assigned to the CPU, it will select the highest priority slack-consumer (a long job) from the job queue to consume the slack. If there is no slack-consumer in the job queue, the slack-producer job J SR-k in the CPU will select the highest priority short job, J nm , from the queue, if there is any. In this case, the remained slack of J SR-k will not be reduced; instead, the remained computation time of the selected job will be reduced, i.e. we let the highest priority short job J nm execute on the priority of J SR-k . Otherwise, J SR-k expires at its deadline and its slack is wasted. By this means, we transfer the slack of J SR-k to that of J SR-n (the slack-reuse job from J nm ) for later use by assigning the expiration time of the slack to be the greater value of the deadlines of J nm and J SR-k , which may extend the lifetime of the slack.

The computation time c ij of a long job J ij from transaction T i is divided into two parts: c ij = c i + ij , where c i is the guaranteed computation time from SML-OPT to T i , and ij is the extra computation time required by the long job. The execution of J ij is also divided into two parts. Firstly, it is allowed to follow its initial priority for using the CPU for a total computation time of c i . For the remaining computation time ( ij ), it has to be provided by slack-providers using the priorities of the slack-providers. To prevent a long job from intruding the executions of lower priority jobs, we maintain a GCT time counter to accumulate the CPU time that a long job has used, excluding the extra slack provided by slack-reuse jobs. Once the GCT time counter reaches the guaranteed computation time (i.e. c i for T i ), there will be possibility of intrusion on lower priority transactions if it continues execution at its original priority. For example, in Figure 3(b), if computation time of J 31 is the same as GCT 3 , and J 22 executes its 22 at its own priority, then it grabs the CPU time that is supposed to be assigned to J 31 (i.e., time slot [7,8]), which forces J 31 to miss its deadline at time 8. Thus, after the GCT time counter has reached the guaranteed computation time, we degrade the priority of the job by increasing its priority number by m (the total number of periodic transactions) to prevent it from infringing upon any lower priority jobs. Please note that before the degradation of priority level, the service to a job for the two parts, i.e. c i and ij , can be interleaved. After the degradation of priority level, the remaining c can only be executed by slack-providers or when system is idle.

It can be seen that the slack-reuse mechanism ensures that a lower priority long job can use slack from higher priority jobs, and a higher priority job can also use slack from lower priority jobs while they do not infringe upon each other's guaranteed computation times.

div.head: Performance Studies
div.p: In this section, we report the results of the performance studies on SML-BA, SML-OPT, and SML-SR, and compare their performance with ML and HH.

div.head: System Settings and Performance Measures
div.p: The simulation model consists of a single CPU system with all real-time objects residing in main memory. Update transactions periodically refresh real-time data objects. The three parameters for each update transaction: validity interval V i , service rate µ i and the requested QoS * i Q , are generated following normal distribution. The service rate of a transaction is the inverse of the mean computation time (E(C i ) in Table 3) of the jobs of the transaction. The computation time of J ij is generated following normal distribution N(1/µ i , 2 ). Since the main purpose of the SML schemes is to improve the schedulability of the update transactions while maximize the QoS of the real-time data objects, we vary the number of update transactions in the experiments. The service rates and validity intervals of the transactions are generated with mean values of 0.1 and 6000 respectively. The validity intervals of X i of the data objects are varied in the range [4200, 7800] according to normal distribution. The assignment of QoS requirement to a real-time data object is randomly generated using the mean QoS value defined Table 3. Table 3

div.head: Experimental Results
div.p: Figures 4 to 6 show the results when the number of transactions varies from 10 to 290 for a system where the mean QoS requirement in temporal consistency is 75%. As shown in the figures, although MA_QoS's for HH and ML are both maintained at 100%, the system can only schedule up to 160 and 190 update transactions, respectively, since max i c is used in deriving the deadlines and periods of the transactions. The SML schemes tradeoffs the QoS with the schedulability. As shown in Figure 4, the SML schemes, SML-BA, SML-OPT and SML-SR, can schedule more transactions by degrading QoS. When the requested QoS is 75%, all the SML schemes can schedule up to 290 update transactions while satisfying the requested QoS. For SML-BA, the MA_QoS is maintained around the requested value, 75%. In contrast, MA_QoS's of SML-OPT and SML-SR are maintained at 100% for number of transactions smaller than 190, which is the maximum number of update transactions scheduled by ML.

For the number of transactions greater than 190, the MA_QoS of SML-OPT decreases gradually with an increase in number of transactions (see Fig. 4). It hits the line for SML-BA when number of transactions is 290, which is very close to the maximum number of transactions supported by SML. Note that similar to SML-BA, the MA_QoS provided from SML-OPT is guaranteed. Increasing the number of the transactions makes it more difficult to further improve the QoS and at the same time guaranteeing the transaction deadlines. Thus, MA_QoS decreases and the performance becomes close to SML-BA when the number of transactions is close to 290. As explained in Section 4.3, SML-SR is an extension of SML-OPT. It can provide at least the same level of guaranteed QoS as SML-OPT. However, the MA_QoS obtained from SML-SR is significantly higher than that of SML-OPT when the number of transactions is larger than 190, as shown in Figure 4. SML-SR can schedule more long jobs by reclaiming slacks. Even when the update workload is heavy, the MA_QoS of SML-SR is still maintained at a very high level (around 99.5% for 290 transactions).

Figure 5 shows the total update workload. Consistent with the results from [16], the workload for HH is higher than ML. The higher MA_QoS guaranteed from SML-OPT results in a heavier TUW as shown in Figure 5. The difference in TUW between SML-BA and SML-OPT becomes smaller as the number of transactions increases since the difference in the guaranteed QoS from SML_OPT and SML-BA becomes less with an increase in number of transactions. The workload of SML-SR is higher than those of SML-BA and SML-OPT when the number of transactions is larger than 190. As shown in Figure 6, a large number of slacks are reused in SML-SR to admit more jobs for improving QoS. Figure 7 shows the distribution of QoS levels achieved for each transaction in SML-SR when there are 290 transactions. Consistent with our expectation, the achieved QoS for transactions with lower priority are higher, i.e., almost 100%, since they are more likely to take advantage of slacks according to the slack reclaim algorithm in SML-SR. We repeated the experiments with different requested QoS. The experimental results are consistent with previous observations. It has been observed that with a higher requested QoS, the number of transactions that are schedulable is smaller. Figure 8 shows the relationship between number of schedulable transactions and the requested QoS. It shows the tradeoff between schedulability and guaranteed QoS. The number of schedulable transactions using the SML approaches is higher than using HH and ML if the requested QoS is smaller than 100%. If the requested QoS is 100%, the number of transactions from SML is the same as ML because SML reverts to ML. We also varied the required QoS, e.g. 85%; we observed similar results. It should be noted that if the requested QoS is lower, the difference in performance between SML and ML is larger. When a smaller deviation in computation time is used, the discrepancy will also be smaller.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Real-time database systems in which time validity intervals are associated with the data objects are discussed in [4][5] [7][8] [13][15] [16]. In [7][8], real-time data semantics are investigated and SSP (Similarity Stack Protocols) are proposed. The correctness of SSP is based on the concept of similarity. Data-deadline is proposed in [15]. Data-deadline based scheduling, forced-wait and similarity based scheduling policies are proposed to maintain temporal consistency of real-time data and meet transaction deadlines. A design methodology for guaranteeing end-to-end requirements of real-time systems is presented in [3]. Their approach guarantees end-to-end propagation delay, temporal input-sampling correlation, and allowable separation times between updated output values. However, their solution is based on the assumption that all the periodic tasks have harmonic periods. A QoS management scheme based on adaptive update policy with feedback and admission control is proposed in [5]. It supports guarantees on deadline miss ratio and data freshness (temporal consistency) in the presence of unpredictable workloads and data access patterns.

The work presented in our paper is also related to the work of [4] [16]. Our work is different from the work of [4][16] as we focus on providing quality of service for temporal consistency of real-time data based on statistical scheduling. Our work is also different from statistical rate monotonic scheduling (SRMS) [1] and slack stealing job admission control [2], which study quality of service guarantee of periodic tasks with rate monotonic scheduling algorithm where periods of tasks are fixed and deadlines are the same as their corresponding periods. In our work, we need to derive periods and deadlines of update transactions for quality of service guarantees, and deadline monotonic scheduling algorithm is used for scheduling update transactions as their deadlines are usually less than corresponding periods. In addition, the superperiod technique proposed in [1] is not suitable to our study with large number of update transactions because deadline is less than or equal to corresponding period in our study.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we present the design and evaluation of algorithms for statistical quality of service guarantee of the temporal consistency of real-time data. We propose a suite of SML approaches to tradeoff between QoS of temporal consistency and the number of update transactions that can be scheduled. SML-BA is proposed as the base algorithm for achieving required QoS of temporal consistency for real-time data. SML-OPT capitalizes on the excessive CPU capacity to improve the QoS of SML-BA. Finally, we extend by adding a slack reclaiming scheme (SML-SR) into it. The reclaimed slacks are reallocated for the admission of jobs whose computation times are higher than the guaranteed value. Experiments have been conducted to compare the SML schemes with existing approaches, i.e., ML and HH. It is demonstrated through experiments that SML approaches are effective for trading between the schedulability of transactions and the QoS guaranteed, and SML-SR significantly outperforms SML-BA and SML-OPT for QoS achieved.
